G0A01: RF is non-ionizing. Its effect on the body is heating, like a microwave oven, not radiation poisoning.
G0A02: Exposure depends on power density, frequency (the body absorbs some frequencies more) and duty cycle (how much of the time you transmit). All of them count.
G0A03: You can show compliance by calculation from OET Bulletin 65, by computer modeling, or by measuring with calibrated equipment. All three work.
G0A04: Time averaging = total exposure averaged over a set period (6 minutes controlled, 30 minutes uncontrolled), so short bursts count less than steady carriers.
G0A05: If you exceed the limits you must stop people from being exposed: move the antenna, cut power, or keep people out of the area.
G0A06: No exemption means you must do a full RF exposure evaluation, and the FCC method is OET Bulletin 65.
G0A07: Lower duty cycle = less time on the air, so the average exposure is lower and you can run more power for the same exposure.
G0A08: Do a routine RF exposure evaluation, then keep people out of any high-exposure spots it finds.
G0A09: Field strength needs a calibrated field strength meter with a calibrated antenna. SWR meters and scopes do not measure the field in the air.
G0A10: The fix is to keep the beam from pointing at the neighbor when they are there. Changing antennas does not solve the main-lobe problem.
G0A11: Indoors, people are close to the antenna, so make sure occupied areas stay under the MPE limits.
G0A12: The RF exposure rules cover every station that averages more than one milliwatt. Amateurs are not exempt.
G0B01: Fuses and breakers go only in the hot wires. Never fuse the neutral or the ground; opening them would leave the hots live.
G0B02: A 20 amp breaker needs at least AWG 12 wire. Remember: 14 gauge = 15 amps, 12 gauge = 20 amps.
G0B03: AWG 14 wire is rated for 15 amps, so use a 15 amp fuse or breaker. A bigger breaker lets the wire overheat.
G0B04: The lightning ground goes outside the building, so the strike's current never comes indoors.
G0B05: A GFCI trips when current leaks from a hot wire straight to ground (maybe through you). Hot to neutral is normal load current.
G0B06: The National Electrical Code covers electrical safety: wiring, grounding, breakers. It says nothing about RF exposure or bandwidth.
G0B07: A harness must be rated for the climber's weight and still within its service life. An expired or overloaded harness can fail.
G0B08: Lock out and tag every circuit that powers devices on the tower before climbing, so no one can switch it on while you are up there.
G0B09: Generators make carbon monoxide, so run them only in a well-ventilated area, never indoors.
G0B10: The danger of lead solder is lead on your hands getting into food. Wash after soldering.
G0B11: All ground rods must be bonded together with the station's other grounds, so lightning cannot create a voltage difference between them.
G0B12: An interlock cuts the dangerous voltage when the cabinet is opened, so you cannot touch it by accident.
G0B13: Arrestors go where the feed lines enter the building, so a surge is sent to ground before it comes inside.
G1A01: General can't use all of 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters: each has an Extra-only slice at the bottom. Same four bands as G1A08.
G1A02: 30 meters is CW and data only. No phone at all.
G1A03: 30 meters is narrow (50 kHz) and limited to CW and data, so no images either.
G1A05: 7.125 to 7.175 MHz is the Extra-only part of the 40 meter phone segment. General phone on 40 starts at 7.175.
G1A06: Secondary means you must not interfere with the primary users and must accept their interference.
G1A07: CW is allowed everywhere on every amateur band, so General can send CW across the entire 10 meter band.
G1A08: 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters each have a bottom slice only Extras can use.
G1A09: 15 meters runs 21.000 to 21.450 MHz, and General phone is 21.275 to 21.450, so 21300 kHz = 21.300 MHz fits. The other choices are on 20, 17 and 12 meters.
G1A10: 10 meter repeaters live above 29.5 MHz, near the top of the band.
G1A11: Extras get the bottom of each phone segment, so General gets the upper part.
G1B01: Up to 200 feet you need no FAA notice or FCC registration (unless you are near a public-use airport).
G1B02: Only one beacon per band from the same location.
G1B03: Beacons exist so hams can observe propagation and reception.
G1B04: Occasionally relaying US government weather and propagation forecasts is allowed. Unidentified tests and encryption are not.
G1B05: One-way Morse code practice transmissions are allowed. Unidentified tests and sales ads are not.
G1B06: PRB-1: local rules must reasonably accommodate amateur antennas and be the minimum needed for a legitimate local purpose.
G1B07: Abbreviations and procedural signals are fine as long as they don't hide the meaning of the message.
G1B08: You can work any country unless its government has told the ITU it objects to contacts with US amateurs.
G1B09: Automatic beacons on HF are allowed only from 28.20 to 28.30 MHz on 10 meters.
G1B10: A beacon may run up to 100 watts PEP output.
G1B11: The FCC decides what good engineering and good amateur practice means where Part 97 is silent.
G1C01: 10.140 MHz is on 30 meters, where the limit is 200 watts PEP output.
G1C02: 12 meters has the normal amateur limit: 1500 watts PEP output.
G1C03: On 60 meters USB channels, the limit is 2.8 kHz bandwidth.
G1C04: On 60 meters, if your antenna is not a dipole you must keep a record of its gain (power is set as ERP relative to a dipole).
G1C05: General gets the full 1500 watts PEP output on 10 meters (28 MHz).
G1C06: 160 meters (1.8 MHz) allows the full 1500 watts PEP output.
G1C07: A new digital code is legal once its technical characteristics are publicly documented, so others can decode it.
G1C11: Power limits are measured as PEP output from the transmitter.
G1D01: If you once held a General, Advanced or Extra license that was not revoked, you get credit for those elements (you still pass Element 2).
G1D02: A General class VE can give only the Technician exam.
G1D03: With a valid CSCE for General you may use all General and Technician privileges right away, before the database updates.
G1D04: Every exam session needs at least three VEs of General class or higher for a Technician exam.
G1D05: Running a US station remotely from abroad needs only your US operator/primary station license.
G1D06: Until the upgrade shows in the database, add AG whenever you use General privileges.
G1D07: A Volunteer Examiner Coordinator (VEC) accredits VEs, not the FCC directly.
G1D08: A non-citizen can be a VE if they hold an FCC amateur license of General or higher.
G1D09: A CSCE is good for 365 days of element credit.
G1D10: VEs must be at least 18 years old.
G1D11: After the 2-year grace period, show proof of the expired license and pass the current Element 2 (Technician) exam to get it back.
G1D12: You are using a station in another country, so that country's rules apply, not the FCC's.
G1E01: A third party whose amateur license was revoked and not reinstated cannot take part. Citizenship and language don't matter.
G1E02: A 10 meter repeater can relay a Technician's 2 meter signal only if the 10 meter repeater's control operator is General or higher.
G1E03: To reach an automatic digital station outside the auto segments, the station starting the contact must be under local or remote control.
G1E04: Near an FCC monitoring station, on a band where amateurs are secondary, or running spread spectrum: all need care to avoid harmful interference.
G1E05: With a third-party agreement, messages must be about amateur radio, personal remarks, or emergencies and disaster relief.
G1E06: North and South America are ITU Region 2.
G1E07: Amateur stations may not talk to unlicensed Wi-Fi stations anywhere in 2.4 GHz.
G1E08: Spread spectrum is limited to 10 watts PEP output.
G1E10: Those five frequencies (14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930, 28.200 MHz) are the international propagation beacon network.
G1E11: Automatic digital stations may talk to each other anywhere on 6 meters and up, and in limited segments of some HF bands.
G1E12: Remote control changes nothing: third-party messages are fine whenever the rules otherwise allow them.
